351.event_title: Piltdown Man is exposed as a forgery
351.place: Piltdown, Sussex, and the Natural History Museum, London, England, United Kingdom
351.event: In 1912 the amateur geologist Charles Dawson and the palaeontologist Arthur Smith Woodward announced skull and jaw fragments from a gravel pit at Piltdown as an early human ancestor, and many leading scientists accepted it as a missing link between apes and humans. For about forty years the find shaped debate about human origins, and it was one reason why Raymond Dart's genuine 1925 Taung fossil from South Africa was widely doubted. In November 1953 Joseph Weiner, Kenneth Oakley and Wilfrid Le Gros Clark showed that the jaw came from a modern ape, that its teeth had been filed down and that the bones had been stained to look ancient.
351.explanation: A counterfeit taken for the real thing did more than fool individuals: it sent a whole field of research down a false path for decades and caused genuine evidence to be dismissed.
351.tie_back: The kural says that mistaking what is not real for the real is the delusion from which an unworthy chain of consequences is born, and the Piltdown forgery, accepted as real, produced forty years of misdirected science.
351._accuracy_note: A clear case of the false being taken for the real and breeding further error, but the kural's subject is spiritual delusion and rebirth, which a scientific hoax can only mirror.

352.event_title: Wang Yangming's awakening in exile in Guizhou
352.event: After protesting against the imprisonment of officials by a powerful court eunuch, the Ming official and scholar Wang Yangming was beaten and banished in 1506-1507 to a minor post in remote Guizhou. There, in hardship and isolation, he reached in 1508 a sudden philosophical awakening: that the principles of things are to be sought within one's own mind rather than in external objects, as the school of Zhu Xi had taught. He went on to teach the unity of knowing and acting, and his ideas became one of the most influential schools of thought in China and Japan.
352.explanation: Wang's years of confusion about how to find truth ended not through more outward study but through a clear inner insight, which he then spent his life teaching.
352.tie_back: The kural promises that for those freed of delusion and granted stainless sight, darkness gives way to joy, much as Wang's awakening in a bleak exile cleared his long confusion and set the course of his life.
352._accuracy_note: A documented moment of sudden clear insight after long confusion fits well, though Wang's awakening is philosophical rather than the release from rebirth the commentators read into the kural, and the sources do not describe his inner bliss.

353.event_title: Augustine's conversion in the garden at Milan
353.event: In the summer of 386 Augustine, a teacher of rhetoric in Milan who had spent years torn between philosophies and his old way of life, was sitting in a garden with his friend Alypius when he heard a child's voice that seemed to tell him to take up and read. He opened Paul's letters at random, read a passage from Romans, and in his Confessions wrote that at the end of that sentence all the darkness of doubt fled away. He gave up his teaching post and was baptised by Bishop Ambrose at Easter 387.
353.explanation: Augustine's own account presents the end of doubt, not the acquisition of new information, as the turning point after which his whole life changed direction.
353.tie_back: The kural says that for those who have passed beyond doubt into clarity, heaven is nearer than the earth, and Augustine describes exactly such a moment when doubt fell away and he set his life toward God.
353._accuracy_note: Augustine's description of doubt vanishing at a single moment closely matches the kural, though the scene is known chiefly from his own later Confessions.

354.event_title: Al-Ghazali's crisis of certainty and departure from Baghdad
354.event: Al-Ghazali, appointed chief professor at the Nizamiyya college in Baghdad in 1091 and one of the most celebrated scholars of his day, fell into a spiritual crisis in 1095 in which his voice failed and he could no longer lecture. He left his post and Baghdad, travelled to Damascus and Jerusalem, and turned to the Sufi path. In his later book The Deliverer from Error he described how he had come to doubt whether the senses, and even reason, could give certain knowledge, and how certainty returned only as a gift of God rather than through argument.
354.explanation: One of the most learned men of the medieval Islamic world concluded that neither sense-knowledge nor scholarship was enough without a deeper grasp of the truth.
354.tie_back: The kural says that even full mastery of what the five senses can know brings no benefit without knowledge of reality, which is close to the conclusion al-Ghazali reached when he found sense perception and learning alone could not give him certainty.
354._accuracy_note: Al-Ghazali's documented doubt about the senses maps closely onto the kural's claim, though scholars note that his autobiography was written later as a defence of his choices.

355.event_title: Oskar Pfungst discovers the secret of Clever Hans
355.event: Clever Hans, a horse owned by the Berlin schoolteacher Wilhelm von Osten, appeared to answer arithmetic and other questions by tapping his hoof, and in 1904 a group of experts who examined him found no deliberate trickery. The psychology student Oskar Pfungst then ran careful experiments and showed that the horse answered correctly only when the questioner knew the answer and was visible to him. In his 1907 report Pfungst concluded that Hans was reacting to tiny, unintentional movements of the questioner rather than doing sums.
355.explanation: Pfungst succeeded where expert observers had failed because he tested what was really happening instead of trusting how the performance looked; the Clever Hans effect is still taught as a warning in science.
355.tie_back: The kural defines wisdom as seeing the true reality within a thing, whatever it appears to be, and Pfungst looked past the appearance of a counting horse to the real cause of its answers.
355._accuracy_note: An almost literal case of seeing the true nature behind a convincing appearance; the kural's wider spiritual meaning is not captured.

356.event_title: Thomas Merton enters the Abbey of Gethsemani
356.place: Abbey of Gethsemani, Trappist, Kentucky, United States
356.event: Thomas Merton, who graduated from Columbia University in 1938 and was received into the Catholic Church that same year, taught at Columbia's extension school and at St. Bonaventure College before making a retreat at the Trappist Abbey of Gethsemani in 1941. On 10 December 1941 he entered the abbey as a monk, and he remained a member of the community until his death in 1968. His autobiography The Seven Storey Mountain, published in 1948, described his path from a restless student life to the monastery.
356.explanation: Merton's path ran from wide academic learning to a decision to give his life wholly to contemplation, a step he never reversed.
356.tie_back: The kural speaks of those who have learned and, in this life, seen the truth, setting out on a path from which they do not return, and Merton's move from the university to a lifelong monastic vow follows that pattern.
356._accuracy_note: Learning followed by an irreversible commitment fits the outline, but the kural's path of no return means release from rebirth, which no historical event can show.

357.event: In 1896 the teenage student Venkataraman, later known as Ramana Maharshi, was overcome in his uncle's house in Madurai by a sudden fear of death. Lying still as if dead, he inquired into what it was that dies and concluded that his true self was not the body; Britannica describes this as the experience from which he derived his method of self-inquiry, vichara. About six weeks later he left home for the holy hill of Arunachala at Tiruvannamalai, where he lived until his death in 1950.
357.explanation: By his own account the fear of death never returned after that single inquiry, and the rest of his life and teaching grew from it.
357.tie_back: The kural says that once the mind has examined and firmly grasped That Which Is, there is no more need to think of birth, and Ramana's inquiry into the self, the root of his later teaching, is perhaps the closest documented illustration.
357._accuracy_note: Very close in content and even vocabulary to the kural, though details of the experience come from Ramana's own later recollections, and Britannica gives his age as 17 while other accounts say 16.

358.event_title: Pasteur's swan-neck flasks refute spontaneous generation
358.event: From 1859 Louis Pasteur set out to settle whether living microbes could arise on their own from nonliving matter, a belief defended by the naturalist Felix Pouchet. Pasteur boiled broth in flasks whose long, curved necks let in air but trapped dust; the broth stayed clear, but when the neck was broken off it soon swarmed with microbes. In an 1862 paper he argued that the microbes came from germs in the air, not from spontaneous generation.
358.explanation: A careful look at what was really happening removed a long-standing false belief about how life is born and opened the way to germ theory.
358.tie_back: The kural calls birth a folly that true seeing removes; Pasteur's experiments removed a folly about birth itself, the belief that life springs spontaneously from decay, by seeing the true cause.
358._accuracy_note: The link is partly verbal: Pasteur dispelled an error about the origin of life, while the kural speaks of liberation from the cycle of rebirth through knowledge of the Supreme.

359.event_title: Kamo no Chomei writes An Account of My Hut
359.event: Kamo no Chomei, a poet from a family of Shinto shrine officials, became a Buddhist monk at about fifty and withdrew from the capital, living first at Ohara and then in a tiny hut he built in the hills of Hino, southeast of Kyoto. In 1212 he wrote the Hojoki, An Account of My Hut, named for the hut's size of ten feet square. The work first describes the fires, whirlwind, famine and earthquake that had struck Kyoto in his lifetime, then contrasts them with the quiet of his simple life in the hills.
359.explanation: Chomei set the instability of worldly things beside the peace he found once he had let go of house, rank and possessions, and the Hojoki became a classic of Japanese literature on that theme.
359.tie_back: The kural says that one who knows the true support and lets lesser attachments fall away is no longer gripped by sorrows, and Chomei's record of disasters followed by contentment in a ten-foot hut illustrates that loosening of attachment.
359._accuracy_note: A well-documented picture of detachment bringing peace, though a literary retreat from the world shows detachment only in part and says nothing of the true Support the kural names.

360.event_title: The World Health Assembly declares smallpox eradicated
360.event: After a global vaccination and case-finding campaign led by the World Health Organization from 1967, the world's last naturally occurring case of smallpox was found in Somalia in October 1977. Following two further years of searching for cases, a global commission certified eradication in December 1979. On 8 May 1980 the World Health Assembly, in resolution WHA33.3, formally declared that the world was free of smallpox.
360.explanation: Smallpox is the only human disease ever eradicated, which was possible only because the campaign aimed at complete removal of the disease rather than control.
360.tie_back: The kural says the suffering caused by desire, anger and delusion ends only when they are destroyed so completely that even their names are gone, and smallpox ended only when it was rooted out everywhere rather than merely reduced.
360._accuracy_note: This is an analogy only: the event shows the principle of total eradication ending a disease, but has nothing to do with the inner faults the kural names.
